He had checked the almanac three times, trusting the printed numbers more than the gut feeling that had been nagging at him since dawn. The water did not crash; it simply arrived, a heavy, grey curtain rising to swallow the jagged rocks that usually jutted out like broken teeth. The air grew thick, smelling of brine and ancient, rotting kelp, a scent that seemed to cling to the back of his throat. He watched a single gull, confused by the sudden shift in the landscape, circle lazily before diving into the churning foam. The pier groaned under the weight of the rising water, the wooden planks creaking in a rhythm that sounded suspiciously like a heartbeat. Elias pulled his coat tighter, the dampness seeping through the fabric, chilling him to the bone. He thought of the old fishermen who used to say the sea was a living thing, capable of mood and memory, and for the first time, he believed them. The water lapped at the base of the pilings, higher than it had been in decades, erasing the footprints of those who had walked here in the morning. There was a profound loneliness in the scene, a sense that the world had shrunk to just this narrow strip of wood and the endless, hungry water. He turned back toward the village, the path already obscured by the mist, and wondered if he would ever understand the strange, shifting logic of the coast.
